items.followUp: Name five industries in which enzymes are used and give one use in each.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a correct food-industry application.
rubric.description: Food industry use, such as baking, cheese-making or brewing.
rubric.how: Name a food process in which enzymes are used.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a textile-industry application.
rubric.description: Textile industry use, such as removing starch from cloth.
rubric.how: State the textile process or purpose.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a leather-industry application.
rubric.description: Leather industry use, such as dehairing hides.
rubric.how: State a leather-processing use.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a detergent-industry application.
rubric.description: Detergents use enzymes to remove protein or fat stains.
rubric.how: Name a stain type that enzyme-containing detergents help remove.

rubric.why: Awards credit for another valid industrial use.
rubric.description: Paper industry use, such as processing pulp.
rubric.how: Name the industry and its enzyme-related process.

modelAnswer: In the food industry, enzymes are used in processes such as baking, cheese-making and brewing.
In the textile industry, enzymes are used to remove starch from cloth.
In the leather industry, enzymes are used to dehair hides.
In detergents, enzymes help remove protein and fat stains.
In the paper industry, enzymes are used in processing paper pulp.
Any five correct industry uses earn full credit.

items.followUp: Explain how light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Establishes that light is absorbed by photosynthetic pigments.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy in the thylakoid membranes.
rubric.how: Identify the pigment or photosystem that absorbs light.

rubric.why: Recognises the splitting of water and its products.
rubric.description: Water is split, releasing oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons.
rubric.how: State photolysis and at least one product.

rubric.why: Links electron movement to ATP formation.
rubric.description: Excited electrons pass along carriers; their energy is used to form ATP.
rubric.how: Mention electron transport and ATP formation.

rubric.why: Recognises the reducing power produced in the light reaction.
rubric.description: Electrons and hydrogen reduce NADP to NADPH.
rubric.how: Name NADPH or state that NADP is reduced.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light energy and excites electrons.
Water undergoes photolysis, producing electrons, hydrogen ions and oxygen; oxygen is released.
The excited electrons pass through electron carriers, and their energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
Electrons and hydrogen reduce NADP to NADPH.

items.followUp: Trace the movement of electrons in the Z-scheme from water to NADP.

rubric.why: Identifies the first photosystem in the electron pathway.
rubric.description: Light excites electrons in Photosystem II (P680); lost electrons are replaced by electrons from water.
rubric.how: Name PSII/P680 and connect its replacement electrons to water splitting.

rubric.why: Shows the pathway from PSII through carriers to PSI.
rubric.description: Electrons pass through an electron transport chain to Photosystem I (P700), where light excites them again.
rubric.how: Name the carriers and PSI, or state that electrons are excited again at PSI.

rubric.why: Explains the name and/or the final electron acceptor.
rubric.description: Electrons ultimately reduce NADP to NADPH; the energy-level path of the electrons resembles the letter Z, giving the scheme its name.
rubric.how: State the Z-shaped energy-level pattern or identify NADP as the final acceptor.

modelAnswer: In Photosystem II (P680), light excites electrons; electrons lost by PSII are replaced by electrons from the splitting of water.
The electrons pass through electron carriers to Photosystem I (P700), where light excites them again.
They are transferred to NADP, reducing it to NADPH.
When electron energy levels are plotted along this pathway, the rises and falls resemble the letter Z; therefore, it is called the Z-scheme.

items.followUp: Draw and label a stomach, then describe its main parts and inner lining.

rubric.why: Checks the stomach's connection at its entrance.
rubric.description: Shows the oesophagus entering the stomach at the cardiac end.
rubric.how: Label the oesophagus and its opening into the stomach.

rubric.why: Checks identification of the stomach's main regions.
rubric.description: Labels the fundus, body and pyloric region (or cardiac region).
rubric.how: Label at least two principal stomach regions.

rubric.why: Checks the outlet and its connection to the intestine.
rubric.description: Shows the pyloric outlet/sphincter leading to the duodenum.
rubric.how: Label the pyloric sphincter or duodenum at the stomach's exit.

rubric.why: Checks an important feature of the stomach lining.
rubric.description: Shows or describes the folded inner lining (rugae) and/or gastric glands.
rubric.how: Label the folds or gastric glands inside the stomach.

modelAnswer: Draw a J-shaped outline about 8 cm long and 5 cm wide; leave a narrow opening at the upper end and a curved outlet at the lower end.
Draw and label a short oesophagus, about 2 cm long, entering the upper cardiac end; mark the fundus, body and pyloric region.
At the lower outlet, draw and label the pyloric sphincter and a short duodenum, about 2 cm long.
Inside the outline, draw several folds and label them rugae; label the gastric glands in the stomach wall.
The stomach is a muscular sac between the oesophagus and the small intestine; its inner lining contains folds and gastric glands.

items.followUp: Name one important medical book written by Bu-Ali Sina and state its importance.

rubric.why: Recognises Bu-Ali Sina's major medical writing.
rubric.description: He wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, known as The Canon of Medicine.
rubric.how: Name the book or give its accepted title.

rubric.why: Recognises his contribution to medicine.
rubric.description: His work systematised or advanced medical knowledge and was influential in the study of medicine.
rubric.how: State the medical significance of his work or his contribution as a physician.

modelAnswer: Bu-Ali Sina was a renowned physician who wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine).
This influential work organised and advanced medical knowledge and was used as a medical reference for centuries.

items.followUp: What is floriculture, and how is it related to horticulture?

rubric.why: Identifies horticulture as the cultivation or growing of plants.
rubric.description: Horticulture is the science or practice of cultivating plants.
rubric.how: Give the central idea of plant cultivation.

rubric.why: Identifies examples of plants covered by horticulture.
rubric.description: It includes growing fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.
rubric.how: Name at least one relevant plant group.

modelAnswer: Horticulture is the science and practice of cultivating plants.
It includes the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.

items.followUp: Explain one difference between a scientific hypothesis and a scientific theory.

rubric.why: Checks that a theory is understood as an explanatory account.
rubric.description: A theory explains how or why a natural phenomenon occurs.
rubric.how: State the explanatory role of a theory.

rubric.why: Checks that a law describes an observed regularity rather than explaining its cause.
rubric.description: A law describes a repeated natural pattern or relationship; it does not explain why it occurs.
rubric.how: State what a law describes and distinguish it from an explanation.

modelAnswer: A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation of how or why a natural phenomenon occurs.
A scientific law describes a repeated pattern or relationship in nature; it states what happens, not why.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a quantitative and a qualitative observation.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of quantitative observations.
rubric.description: A quantitative observation uses numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: State that it is numerical or measured.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of qualitative observations.
rubric.description: A qualitative observation describes a quality or characteristic without numerical measurement.
rubric.how: State that it is descriptive and non-numerical.

modelAnswer: A quantitative observation is expressed numerically or by measurement, for example, the plant is 12 cm tall.
A qualitative observation describes a quality without numbers, for example, the flower is red.
